strengths: Achieves strong and internally consistent results on the large-scale B3LYP benchmark (Molecule Stability 24.2% vs. 0.8% for EDM and 0.0% for Geo2Seq) and on class-conditional generation (average hit rate 83.3% vs. 25.7%/42.2% for EDM/Geo2Seq), indicating the approach scales and offers useful controllability.

The fourth-node argument (Theorem 1 and Appendix D) rigorously addresses a genuine ambiguity in inertial-frame canonicalization, namely the sign/direction of the principal axes, and the right-handedness/quadrant construction is a sensible, non-trivial fix.

The Nyström-based encoding for injecting pairwise distances is a creative and well-derived design (Appendix C shows the Cholesky/L^{-1}k_i construction) that lets a standard transformer attention score combine relative position (RoPE-3D) and pairwise RBF distance, avoiding custom attention modules.

The overall pipeline (inertial-frame canonicalization + RDKit canonical ordering + hierarchical type-then-coordinate AR with diffusion loss + CFG) is coherent and technically plausible, and the paper clearly distinguishes its invariant/unconstrained modeling from constrained SE(3)-equivariant architectures (Figure 5).
weaknesses: No ablation studies at all. The two central claimed contributions (canonical tokenization and GeoRoPE) are never isolated, so it is impossible to attribute the reported gains to them rather than to the base autoregressive backbone and diffusion loss. Per the review criteria, the central claims are therefore unsupported.

The Nyström encoding's anchor points are critically under-specified. The paper says only that m anchor points are 'sampled' with m<<n, but never states whether they are learned, fixed, or taken from the molecule. More importantly, it is unclear how anchors are determined at generation time when the full molecule is not yet known; if anchors are drawn from the target molecule this leaks information, and if they are fixed the encoding degenerates to a function of absolute coordinates. This undermines both correctness and reproducibility of a core mechanism.

Reproducibility is weak: there are no model sizes/parameter counts, no training hyperparameters, no compute details, no description of how baselines were trained on B3LYP, and no code or data-release statement. The exact conditioning of the denoising network and the CFG implementation (applied to both logits and noise) are also left vague.

Baseline fairness on B3LYP is questionable. Geo2Seq collapses to 10.0% AtomStability and 0.0% Molecule Stability, and EDM drops from 82.0% MolSta on QM9 to 0.8% on B3LYP. Such dramatic collapses suggest the baselines may not have been trained/evaluated under comparable conditions; the paper does not discuss or control for this, so the headline B3LYP comparison may not be apples-to-apples.

Novelty is incremental and the relationship to concurrent work is unclear. Inertial-frame canonicalization is established prior art (Guo et al. 2025; Lu et al. 2025a; Cheng et al. 2025a), and canonical atom ordering relies on RDKit's standard canonical ranking. Cheng et al. (2025b), a very closely related autoregressive 3D molecule generation method, is cited but never clearly differentiated, so the marginal contribution over it is hard to gauge.

Terminology and claims are imprecise: the tokenization is invariant, not 'SE(3)-equivariant,' yet the abstract/introduction repeatedly claim equivariance. The efficiency claim ('highly efficient') for AR is not substantiated, especially since coordinates require iterative diffusion denoising at every atom, and no efficiency/latency comparison is provided.

Presentation problems: Eq. (6) and the attention-score expansion in Eq. (14) are garbled and difficult to parse, and the RoPE-3D rotation matrix (single shared theta_0 across x/y/z pairs) is not clearly defined, making the claimed relative-position property hard to verify.

The class-conditional setup rests on a self-constructed functional-group-ID labeling scheme, and the 'editing' demonstration (Figure 3) is qualitative only, so the practical value of the controllability claims is not fully established.

strengths: Addresses an interesting and underexplored problem—autoregressive modeling for 3D molecule generation—and frames it around concrete data-level (tokenization) and model-level (hybrid discrete/continuous token) challenges.

The Nyström-based encoding is a clever and principled way to inject explicit pairwise-distance (RBF) information into attention via an inner-product construction, and the derivation in Appendix C is correct and reasonably motivated.
The hierarchical autoregressive factorization (predict atom type via cross-entropy, then coordinates via diffusion loss) is sensible and reported to outperform direct coordinate regression.
Empirical results on several datasets (QM9, GEOM-Drugs, B3LYP) are provided, with notably strong class-conditional/hit-rate numbers and high atom-stability on QM9/GEOM-Drugs.
The paper makes a genuine attempt to combine invariance-aware tokenization, geometry-aware attention, and continuous-token diffusion in a single coherent framework.
weaknesses: No ablation studies. The paper's three central contributions—canonical tokenization, GeoRoPE (RoPE-3D + Nyström), and the hierarchical AR/diffusion-loss head—are never isolated. Without ablations it is impossible to attribute the reported gains to any specific component, which undermines the central claims.

The theoretical claims around canonicalization are inconsistent and underspecified. Theorem 1 in the main text requires the fourth node to be 'not on the y-z plane or x-z plane,' whereas Theorem 2 in the appendix requires it to be 'coplanar with the three basis vectors'; the appendix proof instead relies on v not being collinear with Q_{f,0}. These conditions contradict each other, and the handling of ties (largest-distance atom, planar molecules) is not addressed.

Degenerate eigenvalues are dismissed as harmless ('all valid frames are physically equivalent'), but this is false for tokenization: for symmetric molecules (e.g., CO2, CH4, benzene) different valid frames yield different coordinate sequences for the same molecule, breaking the canonicity the entire method depends on. No quantification of how often this occurs is given.

The fourth-node sign rule introduces a discontinuity—small geometric perturbations can flip which atom is selected, changing the token sequence. This is a well-known failure mode of PCA/canonicalization schemes and is not analyzed.

The claimed novelties are largely adapted from prior work: inertial-frame/PCA canonicalization is explicitly attributed to Guo et al. (2025), Lu et al. (2025a), Cheng et al. (2025a), and the canonical atom ordering is standard RDKit canonical ranking. The remaining delta (sign disambiguation + a tie-break heuristic) is modest.

Reproducibility is poor. The paper omits model size/depth, training compute, number of Nyström anchors m and their selection rule, σ, number of diffusion steps, guidance schedules, and hyperparameters. Appendix C defines RBF(i,0),…,RBF(i,m) without specifying what the anchor '0' is or how anchors are chosen consistently across molecules.

Overstated and internally inconsistent claims. The abstract claims 'SOTA on 7 of the 10 evaluation metrics,' while the introduction claims 3 of 6 on QM9/GEOM-Drugs; Table 1 shows InertialAR leading on only 3 of 6 columns (and it is worse than GeoLDM/UniGEM on GEOM-Drugs validity). The B3LYP 'state-of-the-art across all 4 metrics' is against only two baselines (EDM, Geo2Seq), not the strongest methods (e.g., GeoLDM, UniGEM), so the claim is weak.

Baseline tables are incomplete and heterogeneous: many baseline cells are missing (e.g., Valid&Uni for GeoLDM/UniGEM on QM9), and it is unclear whether numbers are reproduced or copied from other papers. This makes the comparisons unreliable.

The 'molecule editing via CFG' claim (Fig. 3) is not supported. Raising the guidance scale in sampling is not editing a given molecule; no controlled experiment demonstrates transformation of a specific input molecule into a target functional group.

Contradictory positioning on efficiency: the paper motivates AR by 'highly efficient' sampling vs. diffusion, yet the method itself uses iterative diffusion denoising for coordinates, so the efficiency advantage is neither measured nor demonstrated (no runtime/sample-count comparisons).

Presentation is sloppy: Equation 15 contains a duplicated expression; notation is inconsistent (M=(t,C) vs G=(z,R) in the appendix); the reference to 'Li and Wang 2025' mislabels Liao & Smidt (2023); 'Langtrum' for Landrum; and several appendix sections (B, E, F) are long textbook-level digressions that dilute the contribution.

The AR ordering derived from RDKit canonical ranking is chemically/geometrically arbitrary, meaning sequentially adjacent atoms may be spatially distant; the paper does not analyze whether this ordering hurts the spatial conditioning the model relies on.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem—extending autoregressive/transformer sequence modeling to 3D molecule generation—with a clean decomposition of the two central challenges (canonical tokenization and hybrid discrete/continuous token modeling).

Introduces a technically interesting GeoRoPE that combines RoPE-3D (with a proven relative-position inner-product property, Eq. 5-7) and a Nyström/RBF approximation encoding so that attention scores explicitly capture both relative position and pairwise distance (Eq. 14), with a sensible block-diagonal projection design (Eq. 12-13).

The hierarchical AR paradigm (predict atom type via cross-entropy, then coordinates via diffusion loss) is a reasonable and well-motivated way to handle hybrid tokens, and integrating classifier-free guidance for controllable generation/molecule editing is practically valuable.

Empirical results are competitive to strong: near-SOTA on QM9/GEOM-Drugs (best Atom Stability 99.3% and Molecule Stability 94.7% on QM9; best AtomSta 87.2% on GEOM-Drugs) and notably strong on the large-scale B3LYP dataset (MolSta 24.2% vs 0.8% for EDM), plus a large margin on class-conditional generation (83.3% average hit rate vs 25.7%/42.2%).
Evaluation uses standard public datasets (QM9, GEOM-Drugs, B3LYP) and established metrics, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: No ablation studies isolating the core technical contributions. The paper never shows what happens without GeoRoPE, without the Nyström encoding, without RoPE-3D, without the hierarchical type/coordinate split, or with naive tokenization. For a methods paper whose novelty rests on these components, this is a serious gap—it is unclear which design choices actually drive the reported gains versus the AR paradigm and scale.

The efficiency motivation is internally inconsistent. The introduction criticizes diffusion for 'computationally intensive iterative sampling,' yet InertialAR uses diffusion loss for coordinates (Eq. 17-18) which requires iterative denoising at inference (Section 3.3). No wall-clock/throughput comparison is provided, so the claimed efficiency advantage is unsupported.

Novelty of the canonicalization is incremental. PCA/inertial-frame canonicalization is already established (Guo et al. 2025; Lu et al. 2025a; Cheng et al. 2025a), and the permutation handling simply invokes RDKit's standard canonical atom ordering (Landrum, 2016). The genuinely new piece (fourth-node sign resolution) is a small addition.

Terminology and correctness concerns in the symmetry claims: tokenization is repeatedly called 'SE(3)-equivariant' while the actual goal is SE(3) invariance via canonicalization. The fourth-node anchor construction assumes an atom 'not on the y-z plane or x-z plane,' which fails for planar molecules (e.g., CO2 or fully coplanar conformers) and for symmetric molecules with degenerate eigenvalues; the paper acknowledges degeneracy only loosely and does not test these failure cases.

Key implementation details for GeoRoPE/Nyström are missing or unclear, hurting reproducibility: the origin and selection of the m anchor points is not specified (and if data-dependent, how they are chosen per molecule and at inference), and it is not explained how the L^{-1}k_i encoding is constructed during autoregressive generation when geometry is being built.

The 'state-of-the-art on 7 of 10 metrics' framing is modest and somewhat overstated in the abstract: InertialAR is not best on QM9 Valid&Uni (92.5 vs GeoLDM 92.7) nor on GEOM-Drugs Validity (96.8 vs GeoLDM 99.3). Absolute Molecule Stability on B3LYP (24.2%) remains low.

The B3LYP comparison is thin (only EDM and Geo2Seq), and Geo2Seq's near-total collapse (10% AtomSta, 0% MolSta) suggests a possible training/setup issue for that baseline, weakening the informativeness of the comparison.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: inconsistent bolding in Table 1 (e.g., G-SchNet's 95.7 and GDM-AUG's 97.6 are bolded despite not being the best), and several reference errors/duplicates (e.g., '[23] Li and Wang 2025' describing Liao & Smidt's Equiformer; duplicated entries).

The conclusion overclaims by framing the method as 'a foundation model for scientific discovery' without supporting evidence, and the class-conditional benchmark is a custom reconstruction (Section 4.2/B.1) that, while applied consistently to baselines, is non-standard.

strengths: Strong and broad empirical validation: InertialAR achieves state-of-the-art results on 8 of 10 unconditional metrics across QM9, GEOM-Drugs, and B3LYP, and on all 5 metrics for class-conditional generation. The B3LYP Molecule Stability result (24.7% vs 0.0% for Geo2Seq) and the class-conditional hit rates (~83% average vs ~40% for baselines) are substantial gains.

The core idea of turning inertial-frame canonicalization into a generation-ready autoregressive tokenization (PCA-based inertial frame plus deterministic RDKit-based atom reordering) is a sensible and, as far as the paper argues, previously unexplored route for AR 3D molecule generation.

The GeoPE construction is well-motivated: ManhattanPE extends rotary-style encoding to the three spatial axes so that attention scores depend only on relative position, and EuclideanPE recovers pairwise RBF distances via a Nyström low-rank approximation, allowing it to be folded into a standard Transformer attention inner product (Eq. 15). The Nyström derivation in Appendix C is correct.

Ablations are informative: the L2-regression vs Diffusion-Loss comparison (Table 6) shows a dramatic collapse (MolSta 94.7 -> 14.2), and the canonicalization ablation (Table 7) shows consistent, if moderate, degradation without it.

The paper is honest about the theoretical limitations of PCA/inertial-frame canonicalization (degenerate principal moments, axis flips) and provides quantitative robustness analyses (Tables 4-5) and a formal proof for the fourth-node sign disambiguation (Appendix D).

Code availability is claimed, and the controllable-generation task with functional-group-derived Molecule Class IDs is a useful, practically motivated benchmark that goes beyond standard unconditional metrics.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The inertial-frame/PCA canonicalization is taken from prior work (Guo et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025a; Cheng et al., 2025a), ManhattanPE is essentially RoPE applied per-axis, EuclideanPE is a Nyström RBF approximation, and Diffusion Loss is from Li et al. (2024a). The contribution is primarily a well-engineered combination rather than a new mechanism or new understanding.

The central claim of a 'unique, SE(3)- and permutation-invariant' tokenization is overstated. The authors themselves cite Dym et al. (2024) showing any finite canonicalization is necessarily discontinuous, and PCA sign flips can change token order. The empirical argument (rare degeneracy/flips) does not justify the strong invariance language used in the abstract and introduction.

Efficiency claims are unsubstantiated and plausibly wrong. The paper motivates AR over diffusion on the grounds of 'highly efficient' sampling, yet each coordinate token is produced by iterative denoising (Diffusion Loss), implying n x (diffusion steps) network evaluations per molecule. No sampling-time, FLOPs, or throughput comparison against diffusion baselines is reported, so the efficiency motivation is unsupported.

Reproducibility is limited. The main text and appendices omit key architecture details (layer counts, hidden dimensions, Nyström anchor count m, sigma, theta_0), training hyperparameters, optimizer settings, and sampling configurations. Without these, the reported numbers cannot be reliably reproduced even with code.

No parameter-count or compute comparison with baselines. It is unclear whether the gains over Geo2Seq, EDM, etc. stem from the proposed method or from a larger/stronger backbone, weakening the attribution of the improvements.

Baseline coverage is thin in the most demanding settings. On B3LYP only EDM and Geo2Seq are compared, and the class-conditional comparison uses only EDM and Geo2Seq; the broader set of strong diffusion models (e.g., GeoLDM, UniGEM, MiDi) is absent from these two key tables.

The class-conditional task, including the Molecule Class ID construction and the Hit Rate metric, is custom and not validated against an established protocol, making cross-paper comparison difficult and raising questions about how favorable the metric is to this particular model.

Presentation issues: some sentences are garbled (e.g., the 'The first possible sign combinations...' passage in Section 3.1), the Figure 2 caption is confusing, and notation (e.g., simultaneous use of z_i^{Euc} as both a positional encoding and an attention component) is at times inconsistent.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent, end-to-end framework for autoregressive 3D molecule generation that integrates canonical inertial-frame alignment, a geometry-aware positional encoding (GeoPE), a hierarchical type/coordinate decoder, and classifier-free guidance. The pipeline is internally consistent and the individual design choices are well motivated.

Empirical results on the standard benchmarks (QM9, GEOM-Drugs) are competitive and in several metrics state-of-the-art: InertialAR attains the best Valid, Atom Stability and Molecule Stability on QM9 and the best Atom Stability on GEOM-Drugs, which is a non-trivial achievement on widely used evaluation protocols.

The manuscript includes component-level ablations (Diffusion Loss vs. direct L2 regression, canonical atom indexing) and a robustness analysis of the inertial frame (perturbation stability, principal-moment degeneracy). The authors also honestly discuss the theoretical non-uniqueness of PCA-based canonicalization and cite the relevant impossibility results, which is a responsible treatment of limitations.

The geometry-aware attention design (ManhattanPE for relative axis-wise geometry plus EuclideanPE as a Nyström RBF feature map) is a reasonable and technically clean way to inject 3D inductive bias into a standard Transformer.
An impact statement is provided and the dual-use risks of generative chemistry are acknowledged.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental. Every major component is borrowed from prior work: inertial-frame/PCA canonicalization (Guo et al. 2025; Lu et al. 2025a; Cheng et al. 2025a, all cited by the authors), RoPE-style per-axis rotary encoding (Su 2021), Nyström RBF kernel approximation (Williams & Seeger 2000), and Diffusion Loss (Li et al. 2024a). The framing as the 'first' generation-oriented inertial tokenization overstates the contribution, and the permutation-invariance property is effectively delegated to RDKit's canonical SMILES ordering rather than to the proposed method.

The central motivation is undermined by the method itself. The introduction argues AR models are preferable to diffusion because diffusion suffers from 'computationally intensive iterative sampling', yet InertialAR generates each atom's coordinates via a diffusion denoising process, i.e., iterative sampling at every token. No runtime, sampling-step, or throughput comparison against diffusion baselines is provided, so the claimed efficiency advantage is unsupported and plausibly false.

The B3LYP 'state-of-the-art across all four metrics' claim is not credible with only two baselines (EDM and Geo2Seq), especially given that Geo2Seq collapses to 2.7% Valid&Unique and 10% AtomStability — numbers far below its reported performance elsewhere and suggestive of a weak reimplementation rather than a genuine comparison. The large-scale claim is therefore weakly evidenced.

Class-conditional results are likewise compared against only two baselines (EDM, Geo2Seq). The reported Hit Rates (~83–91%) are strikingly high, and no analysis of class imbalance, label leakage (classes defined from SMILES functional-group patterns), or the relationship between CFG scale and diversity is given. The molecule-editing results are purely qualitative (three examples).

Reproducibility is insufficient. No model size, training hyperparameters, optimizer/schedule, Nyström anchor count m, anchor sampling strategy, number of denoising steps, inference-time settings, or computational budget are reported. All results appear to be single runs with no variance, error bars, or significance testing, and the 'code available at' URL is absent.

A fundamental design question is not addressed: the canonical atom order is a global function of the molecular graph (RDKit canonicalization uses connectivity, ring membership, etc.), which is unknown while the molecule is being built sequentially. The paper does not explain how this graph-dependent, global ordering is realized at generation time, nor how variable-length generation is terminated (no end-of-sequence token is described), despite claiming 'flexible variable-sized generation'.

Several reporting inconsistencies weaken confidence: the abstract claims SOTA on '8 of the 10' metrics while the introduction says '4 of 6' and the B3LYP section says 'all 4', and margins over baselines are marginal in several places (e.g., 97.3 vs. 97.1 Valid on QM9; 99.2 vs. 99.0 AtomSta). The fourth-node sign-disambiguation scheme is a heuristic whose guarantee requires distinct principal moments and non-degenerate anchor conditions, validated only empirically.

strengths: The paper introduces a coherent and somewhat novel framing: applying inertial-frame canonicalization specifically as a generation-ready tokenization for autoregressive 3D molecule generation, which is a reasonable and under-explored direction relative to diffusion-based approaches.

The GeoPE design is technically clean: combining a RoPE-style per-axis Manhattan encoding (Eq. 6-7) with a Nyström-approximated RBF distance bias (Eq. 8-9, App. C) yields an attention score that decomposes into Manhattan relative-geometry plus Euclidean-distance terms (Eq. 15), which is a sensible and well-motivated inductive bias.

The empirical results are broadly strong and cover multiple scales: SOTA on most reported metrics for QM9, GEOM-Drugs, and especially the large-scale B3LYP benchmark, plus large margins in class-conditional generation (Table 3).

The paper is honest about the known theoretical weaknesses of inertial-frame canonicalization (degenerate eigenvalues, axis-flip discontinuities) and provides an empirical robustness analysis (Section E.1, Tables 4-5) rather than overclaiming theoretical perfection.
Useful component-wise ablations: Diffusion Loss vs. direct L2 regression (Table 6) shows a dramatic and convincing collapse of L2 regression, and the canonicalization ablation (Table 7) is reported.
The impact statement appropriately flags dual-use risks of generative chemistry and recommends safety screening.
weaknesses: The permutation-invariance contribution—presented as a core pillar of the method—is only weakly supported by evidence. Table 7 shows that removing RDKit canonicalization reduces Valid by only 0.4 points and Valid&Unique by 2.5 points, which is inconsistent with the strong emphasis on eliminating the n! permutation ambiguity. This undercuts one of the two stated tokenization contributions.

The generation-time consistency of the canonical frame is not addressed. The canonical inertial frame depends on the full molecule's geometry (center of mass, inertia tensor, anchor node), but AR generation is sequential and the frame is unknown during sampling. The manuscript does not explain how the model produces coordinates consistent with a canonical frame it cannot yet compute, nor does it analyze the resulting self-consistency / frame-mismatch error.

The B3LYP comparison is thin and potentially unreliable. Only two baselines are used, and one (Geo2Seq) collapses to 2.7% Valid&Unique, which is unexplained and could indicate dataset-handling or protocol issues (e.g., >50 atom types, weights up to 1000, differing tokenization). MolSta of 24.7% is low in absolute terms and is not contextualized.

Some SOTA claims are overstated. InertialAR is not the best on QM9 Valid&Unique (92.5 vs. UniGEM 93.2) nor on GEOM-Drugs Valid (98.0 vs. GeoLDM 99.3). The abstract's '8 of 10' and intro's '4 of 6' framing also reads as metric cherry-picking, and the two statements are inconsistently worded.

Conditional-generation baselines are limited and fairness is unclear. Only EDM and Geo2Seq are compared, and it is not explained how a diffusion model (EDM) was made class-conditional under the newly defined Molecule Class ID scheme, nor whether all baselines were trained with matched conditioning. The very large hit-rate gap (83.3% vs. ~25%) warrants scrutiny.

The most directly relevant concurrent work (Cheng et al., 2025b, 'Scalable autoregressive 3D molecule generation') is cited but not benchmarked, which weakens the claimed positioning as the first generation-oriented inertial-frame tokenization for AR modeling.

Reproducibility is limited. The code link is empty in the manuscript, and key details are missing: Nyström anchor-point selection (data-dependent vs. fixed, how m and sigma are set), block-diagonal weight initialization, model dimensions/layer counts, parameter counts, and training compute. These are needed for others to build on the method.

The EuclideanPE branch is effectively a scalar distance-bias added to the attention logit (Eq. 15), which is closer to a Graphormer-style distance bias than a positional encoding; the framing as 'positional encoding' slightly overstates the mechanism, and the interaction between the additive scalar RBF term and the query/key scaling is not discussed.

Evaluation scope is inconsistent across settings (e.g., 6 metrics in Table 1 vs. 4 in Table 2 vs. 5 in Table 3), and the paper does not report uniqueness separately or error bars/variance across seeds, making the strength of the gains hard to gauge.
